content.chapter: Chapter 1: The First Linguistic Study of Turkic
objectives: Explain what kind of study Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is.
Define a dialect in the words of the book.
Say what the work aimed to do and what it shows about its author.
Use the passive (was written / was prepared) and which.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter defines the work and the key word ‘dialect’. A definition box (term → definition → example) helps learners handle the academic tone, and the passive appears naturally because the book is the topic.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The work is a dictionary from Turkic dialects to Arabic, not from Arabic to Turkic.
“Knowledgeable about dictionaries” means he knew the dictionaries in Arabic and Persian; he did not write them.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past simple passive · which (non-defining) · both … and · just as … as
Notice (Activity 1): It was written by Mahmud Kashgari.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *It was wrote · *which it means · *both Arabic or Persian.
Use (Activity 4): dialects in my country.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: lin-GUIS-tic, DI-a-lect, com-pre-HEN-sive, KNOWL-edge-a-ble.
Names: ka-ra-KHA-nid, mah-MUD kash-GA-ri.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do people in different parts of your country speak in different ways?”
duringReading: First reading: What kind of work is this?
Second reading: complete the definition box for “dialect”.
Find two things the work shows about Kashgari.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Definition box; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: dialects; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is the work called the first linguistic study of Turkic?
What does the work include?
What does the content show about Kashgari’s knowledge?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Dictionary of Dialects” and “Turkic to Arabic” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: linguistic, dialect, comprehensive content, advanced, knowledgeable.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the definition box with the term filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a dictionary entry for the word “dialect” with an example from your country.

formativeAssessment: Explains what kind of study it is.
expectedResponses: Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is the first linguistic study of Turkic. It was written by Mahmud Kashgari and prepared as a dictionary from Turkic dialects to Arabic, which shows that he knew both Arabic and Persian well.
content.transferTask: Write about a dialect or accent you know.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the book’s definition of a dialect?

exitTicket: Write one passive sentence about the book.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains what kind of study it is.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain in three sentences what Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is and why it was written. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each explains the main idea and one detail. The partner asks one follow-up question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the definition of a dialect. Asker asks “What three things does a dialect have?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “What is a dialect? Do you have dialects in your country?” The learner explains and gives an example.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “It aimed to teach the Turkic language to Arabs and prove that it is just as rich as Arabic.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is and what a dialect is. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer define ‘dialect’ in the first chapter?” (Because the title of the book is about dialects.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain “dialect” in their own words and give both aims of the book.

thinkAloud.sentence: A dialect is a regional form of a language with its own special vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “A dialect is” tells me this is a definition. The next sentence starts with “So”, so it uses the definition to explain the book’s title. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “It was written by Mahmud Kashgari in 11th-century Karakhanid Turkish.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: In which language and century was it written?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences about a dialect you know.
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate one question about his or her dialect.

objectives: Describe where Kashgari was born and died, with the book’s level of certainty.
Explain his family background.
Retell how he describes himself.
Use It is generally believed that and one of the + superlative.
content.pedagogy: The chapter mixes facts (dates) with a common view (the place of birth) and the author’s own words about himself. Learners notice how the text shows certainty and how a self-description uses superlatives.
priorKnowledge: Relative clauses with who and which.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Kashgari was born in Barsgan and died in Kashgar; learners often mix them up.
Nasr Ilig Khan was Kashgari’s ancestor, not his father.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: It is generally believed that · one of the + superlative + plural noun · belongs to
Notice (Activity 1): It is generally believed that …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *one of the best thrower · *It generally believes.
Use (Activity 4): a short profile.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: BARS-gan, KASH-gar, NASR i-LIG KHAN, ma-ve-ra-ün-ne-HIR.
Stress: AN-ces-tor, au-TON-o-mous.
beforeReading: Ask: “How would you describe yourself in one sentence?”
duringReading: First reading: Where was Kashgari born?
Second reading: make a profile card: born / died / family / skills.
Find four things he says about himself.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Profile card; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a short profile; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the writer say “It is generally believed”?
Who was Nasr Ilig Khan?
What do Kashgari’s words about himself tell us?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Kashgar” and “Nasr Ilig Khan” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: East Turkestan, belongs to, ancestor, Transoxiana, spear throwers.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the profile card with the headings.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write Kashgari’s profile in six sentences for a museum card.

formativeAssessment: Describes where he was born and died.
Uses one of the + superlative correctly.
expectedResponses: It is generally believed that Kashgari was born in Barsgan and died in Kashgar. He came from a noble family, and his ancestor was Nasr Ilig Khan. He says he is one of the clearest speakers.
content.transferTask: Write a short profile of a person you admire.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the difference between facts and a common view?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “one of the” + superlative about Kashgari.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners give a short profile of Mahmud Kashgari. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner where Kashgar is today. The partner restates it with “is located in”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 2. Asker asks “Who was his famous ancestor?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A journalist interviews Kashgari’s biographer: “What did Kashgari say about himself?” The learner answers with reported speech.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Kashgari says that he belongs to a noble family, and his ancestor was Nasr Ilig Khan, the famous Karakhanid ruler who conquered Transoxiana and Bukhara.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, who Mahmud Kashgari was and what he said about himself. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer use ‘It is generally believed’ about his birthplace?” (It is not completely certain.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give both dates and report two of Kashgari’s claims with “He says that …”.

thinkAloud.sentence: He also says he is one of the Turks who know the language best, one of the clearest speakers, one of the wisest, and one of the best spear throwers.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “He says” tells me these are Kashgari’s own claims. The pattern “one of the … -est” repeats four times. I can make a list of four qualities. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Mahmud Kashgari was born in 1008 and died in 1105.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Where was he probably born?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: What would you say about yourself in a short profile?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

objectives: Describe how the Dîvân was written, improved and presented.
List what the work contains.
Explain why it can be seen as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.
Use after + -ing and the linkers After that, In addition and For this reason.
content.pedagogy: A factual chapter with a clear timeline and a long list. A timeline plus a “What is inside?” mind map lets learners organize the information before they explain the conclusion: an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Kashgari presented the work in 1077, three years after he completed it.
An encyclopedia here means a work with information about nearly every aspect of life, not a modern book series.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: after + -ing · After that · In addition · For this reason · can be seen
Notice (Activity 1): after improving it several times …
Build (Activities 2–3): link the facts, then correct errors.
Likely errors: *after improve · *The work contain.
Use (Activity 4): how I finished a project.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: muk-te-DÎ bi-em-ril-LÂH, ab-BA-sid.
Stress: en-cy-clo-PE-di-a, PROV-erbs, ID-i-oms.
beforeReading: Ask: “What can you find in a good encyclopedia?”
duringReading: First reading: When did Kashgari begin and complete the work?
Second reading: draw a timeline and a mind map of what is inside.
Find why it can be seen as an encyclopedia.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–18 Timeline and mind map; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a project; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Kashgari do between 1072 and 1074?
To whom did he present the work?
Why can the work be seen as an encyclopedia?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Baghdad, 1077” and “An Encyclopedia” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: related to.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the timeline with the three years marked.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short book review of the Dîvân using the information in the chapter.

expectedResponses: Kashgari began the work in 1072. After improving it several times, he completed it in 1074 and presented it in Baghdad in 1077. It has information about nearly every aspect of life, so it can be seen as an encyclopedia.
content.transferTask: Write about a project you finished.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link the list of contents to the idea of an encyclopedia?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “after + -ing” about Kashgari.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how the Dîvân was written and why it can be called an encyclopedia. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads up to “in 1077” and B reads the rest. Each explains the main idea. Together they make a time line.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence with “It also includes”. Asker asks “What else does the book include?” Checker checks three items.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A librarian asks, “Is this book only a dictionary?” The learner explains why it is more than that.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “For this reason, the work can be seen as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Kashgari wrote his book and what it contains. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What evidence does the writer give before calling it an encyclopedia?” (It has words, poetry, grammar, names, traditions, beliefs and legends.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the three dates in order and three kinds of content.

thinkAloud.sentence: For this reason, the work can be seen as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “For this reason” tells me this is a conclusion. The reason is the long list before it. The book has information about nearly every part of life. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “The work contains about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: To whom did he present his work in 1077?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: What would you put in an encyclopedia of your culture?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one more idea.

objectives: Report what Kashgari writes about the Turks, using reporting verbs.
Describe his journey: when, how long and why.
Name the dialects he learned.
Use owing to, until and reporting verbs.
content.pedagogy: The chapter reports Kashgari’s views and a hadith he records, then describes his long journey. Reporting verbs (states, writes, records, adds) keep a clear line between the author’s words and the narrator.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The views in the first paragraph are what Kashgari writes; the narrator reports them.
He traveled for ten or fifteen years before he arrived in Baghdad, not after.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: owing to + noun · until + clause · reporting verbs (state, write, record, add)
Notice (Activity 1): Owing to this belief and confidence …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose reporting verbs, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *owing to he believed · *He states me that.
Use (Activity 4): my research trip.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: O-ghuz, CHI-gil, YAG-ma, kyr-GYZ, TURK-men.
Stress: MOD-es-ty, BRAV-er-y, CON-fi-dence.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do people travel to learn something?”
duringReading: First reading: What does Kashgari write about the Turks?
Second reading: make a journey card: start / time / end / what he collected.
Find the six groups whose dialects he learned.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Journey card; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a research trip; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What qualities of the Turks does Kashgari describe?
Why did he start his journey?
Why was it important to visit so many tribes?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Journey” and “The Dialects” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: qualities, long-lasting kingdom, Owing to.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the journey card with the start year filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short diary entry by Kashgari on his journey.

formativeAssessment: Reports Kashgari’s views with a reporting verb.
Uses owing to or until correctly.
expectedResponses: Kashgari writes that the Turks have many good qualities. Owing to this belief, he left his home in 1057 and traveled from tribe to tribe until he arrived in Baghdad, collecting material for his work.
content.transferTask: Plan a research trip about language or culture in your region.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep Kashgari’s words separate from the narrator’s?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “owing to” and one with “until”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain Kashgari’s belief about the Turks and how he collected his material. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each explains the main idea. The partner asks a follow-up question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the list of dialects. Asker asks “Which dialects did he learn?” Checker checks six names.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A student asks, “How did Kashgari collect so many words?” The learner explains his journey.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “During this time, he collected the material that he needed for his work.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why Kashgari traveled and what he collected. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer say ‘Owing to this belief and confidence’?” (It links the hadith with the start of his journey.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the year 1057, the length of the journey and three dialects.

thinkAloud.strategy: Link a reason and an action
thinkAloud.sentence: Owing to this belief and confidence, he started his journey and began to visit all Turkic countries.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Owing to” means “because of”. “This belief” points back to the hadith. So the hadith is the reason for the journey. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “He then describes many good qualities of the Turks, such as beauty, bright faces, good manners, modesty, bravery, and respect for elders.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: When did Kashgari leave his home?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Which good qualities do you want people to see in your community?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Oghuz and the Caliph
objectives: Explain why the Oghuz get the most attention in the book.
Explain the link between the Seljuks, the Abbasids and the caliph.
Name the three great Turkic states of the time.
Use probably, It is likely that and The reason why … is that.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from facts to careful interpretation. Learners see how a writer explains causes without claiming more than the evidence shows, a key skill for B1 reading and writing.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The writer says the reason is “probably” the power of the Seljuks; it is an explanation, not a proven fact.
Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasids, not of the Seljuks.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: probably · It is likely that · The reason why … is that · not only … (but also)
Notice (Activity 1): It is likely that Kashgari was aware …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *The reason why … is because · *It is likely Kashgari aware.
Use (Activity 4): a careful explanation.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: SEL-juks, GHAZ-na-vids, ka-ra-KHA-nids, ab-BA-sids.
Stress: po-LIT-i-cal, PROB-a-bly.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do some groups in history get more attention than others?”
duringReading: First reading: Which tribe gets the most attention?
Second reading: make a cause chart: strong Seljuks → protect Abbasids → attention to the Oghuz.
Find the three great Turkic states.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Cause chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a careful explanation; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What information does the book give about the Oghuz?
Why was it important that the book was finished in Baghdad?
How sure is the writer about the reason?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Oghuz” and “Three Great States” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: tribes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the cause chart with the first box filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph about the Oghuz using both facts and careful explanations.

formativeAssessment: Explains why the Oghuz get attention.
Uses probably or It is likely that.
expectedResponses: The Oghuz get the most attention in the book. The reason is probably that the Seljuks, an Oghuz tribe, were very strong and protected the Abbasids. It is likely that Kashgari knew about the Turks’ political power.
content.transferTask: Explain why something is popular in your school or town.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners separate facts from careful explanations?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “probably” and one with “It is likely that”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why the Oghuz get attention.
Uses probably or It is likely that.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why the Oghuz get so much attention in the book. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner why it was important that the book was finished in Baghdad. The partner restates it with “because”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last sentence. Asker asks “What were the three great Turkic states?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A history student asks, “Why did Kashgari write so much about the Oghuz?” The learner answers carefully, using “probably”.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The Oghuz are the Turkic tribe that gets the most attention in the book.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, who the Oghuz were and why Kashgari wrote so much about them. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer uses ‘probably’ and ‘It is likely’. What does this show?” (The reasons are the writer’s careful guesses.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners use “probably” or “It is likely that” and name the Seljuks as an Oghuz tribe.

thinkAloud.sentence: The reason why Kashgari drew so much attention to this tribe is probably that the Seljuks, an Oghuz Turkic tribe, were very strong and protected the Abbasids, the center of the Islamic world.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Probably” tells me this is not a sure fact. The writer gives a good reason, but I should present it as a guess. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “He writes the names of twenty-two of the twenty-four Oghuz tribes.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: How many Oghuz tribes did he name?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences about a group of people that you would like to describe in a book.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

objectives: Explain why Kashgari praised Turkish.
Describe the status of Arabic in schools and among scholars.
Say what Kashgari believed about his mother tongue.
Use make + person + base verb and believe in.
content.pedagogy: A short chapter with one clear cause → result: Arabic was dominant, so Kashgari wanted to praise Turkish. It invites learners to think about their own mother tongue with respect for other languages.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Kashgari did not reject Arabic; he wanted to show that Turkish could compete with it.
“Dominant” means the strongest and most used, not the only language.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: make + person + base verb · believe in · could (ability)
Notice (Activity 1): made Kashgari praise …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct errors.
Likely errors: *made him to praise · *believe on.
Use (Activity 4): in praise of my language.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: DOM-i-nant, STA-tus, RICH-ness, com-PETE.
Linking: “mother tongue” /ˈmʌðər tʌŋ/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which languages do people use for science today? Why?”
duringReading: First reading: Which language was dominant?
Second reading: draw cause → result.
Find what Kashgari believed.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–15 Cause and result; 15–19 Quick Challenge; 19–34 Language Focus 1–3; 34–42 Use: in praise of my language; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why was Arabic the main language for teaching?
What did the status of Arabic make Kashgari do?
What does it mean that Turkish “could compete with Arabic”?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Arabic in Schools” and “His Mother Tongue” when the picture is in place.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the cause → result frame.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short speech by Kashgari praising Turkish.

expectedResponses: Arabic was dominant in schools, and scholars wrote their books in Arabic. This made Kashgari praise Turkish, because he believed in the richness of his mother tongue.
content.transferTask: Write in praise of your mother tongue.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners show respect for both languages?

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why Kashgari praised Turkish. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner explains the chapter to a partner. The partner says it in one sentence with “because”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last sentence. Asker asks “What did Kashgari believe about his mother tongue?” Checker checks both beliefs.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A friend asks, “Why should we use our home language for science too?” The learner answers with Kashgari’s example.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The scholars of that time also wrote their books in Arabic.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why Kashgari wanted to praise his mother tongue. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What does ‘compete with Arabic’ mean here?” (Turkish could be as rich and useful as Arabic.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain the high status of Arabic and Kashgari’s two beliefs.

thinkAloud.sentence: This high status of Arabic made Kashgari praise his own language, Turkish, because he believed in the richness of his mother tongue and that it could compete with Arabic.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “This high status” points back to the first two sentences. “Made … praise” shows a cause and an effect. “Because” adds his personal reason. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “In the schools of the Karakhanid and Transoxiana cultural centers, Arabic was dominant and the main language for teaching.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: In which language did scholars write their books?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences about why your home language is rich.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one example.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: The Importance of the Map
objectives: Describe Kashgari’s map: center, design, colors and limits.
Explain how the map reflects Kashgari’s belief.
Explain why the map is important today.
Use while (contrast), is considered and as far … as.
content.pedagogy: The chapter describes a map, so learners can build it on the board as they read. It also shows how a map reflects a point of view: Kashgari put the Turkic homeland at the center, which the book links to his belief.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Balasagun is in the heart of the Turkic land on the map; it is not the capital of the Abbasids.
“Jabarqa” is Japan; “the Land of Yecüc and Mecüc” is China.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: while (contrast) · is considered · as far … as · according to
Notice (Activity 1): …, while China is shown as …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *as far west than · *according with.
Use (Activity 4): the center of my map.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ba-la-sa-GUN, ja-BAR-qa, I-dil, e-thi-O-pi-a.
Stress: car-TOG-ra-pher, ge-o-GRAPH-i-cal, per-SPEC-tive.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is in the center of the maps you know? Why?”
duringReading: First reading: What is in the center of the map?
Second reading: draw the map with the colors and limits.
Find why the map is important today.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–20 Draw the map; 20–23 Quick Challenge; 23–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–42 Use: the center of my map; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is Kashgari known as the first Turkic cartographer?
How does the map reflect his belief?
Why is the map important today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Balasagun” and “Jabarqa” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: document.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a circle with the center marked.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a museum label for Kashgari’s map in 60 words.

formativeAssessment: Explains the link with his belief.
Uses while or as far … as correctly.

metadata.title: Mahmud Kashgari B1 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Mahmud Kashgari and His Work Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk (Kaşgarlı Mahmud)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 11 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected texts about history, language and culture, and who can produce supported explanations and short reflections.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through Mahmud Kashgari and Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk: the author’s life and journey, the work and its purpose, the Oghuz, the world map, the Twelve-Animal calendar and Nowruz, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 11 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: definition, timeline, cause and result, reported views, a legend or a list.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: past simple passive · which (non-defining) · both … and · just as … as
Ch2: It is generally believed that · one of the + superlative + plural noun · belongs to
Ch3: after + -ing · After that · In addition · For this reason · can be seen
Ch4: owing to + noun · until + clause · reporting verbs (state, write, record, add)
Ch5: probably · It is likely that · The reason why … is that · not only … (but also)
Ch6: make + person + base verb · believe in · could (ability)
Ch7: while (contrast) · is considered · as far … as · according to
Ch8: first conditional · let us + verb · However / Therefore / so · be named after
Ch9: ordinal numbers · X means Y · be named after (from Chapter 8)
Ch10: some …, while others … · when + present, present · present perfect with since · still continue
Ch11: be regarded as · passive with by · still + present simple (still exists)

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people, places and key events.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, timelines, causes and results, reported views and the writer’s certainty.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe people, places and traditions, explain causes and report views.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, linking words and chapter patterns.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — Respect for elders and for one’s own and other languages.
D3 Diligence — Long, patient work to reach a goal.
D16 Responsibility — Thinking about the people who come after us.
languageFocus: Every one of the 11 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts and timelines given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
The beliefs about the meaning of each year belong to the old Turkic calendar; present them as old beliefs, not as rules or predictions for today.
The hadith and the sentences about Allah in Chapters 4 and 7 belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are, without extra comment.
Chapter 5 says “probably” and “It is likely that”; present these as the writer’s careful explanations, not as proven facts.
Bracketed Turkish words and old Turkic names belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Mahmud Kashgari’s dictionary links the 11th-century Turkic world with questions every community faces today: how to keep a language alive, how to record shared time and how to learn about other nations.

themes.title: Keeping a language alive:
themes.description: Kashgari collected the dialects of many tribes and praised his mother tongue (Chapters 4 and 6). Discuss how people protect languages and dialects today.

themes.title: Shared time:
themes.description: The khan wanted a calendar so that people would agree on dates (Chapter 8). Compare calendars and new year days, such as Nowruz (Chapter 10).

themes.title: Maps and points of view:
themes.description: Kashgari put the Turkic homeland at the center of his map (Chapter 7). Discuss how maps can show a point of view.

themes.title: Working together:
themes.description: Many Turkic states supported the UNESCO celebration (Chapter 11). Discuss how countries share a cultural heritage.

actions: Ask an older family member for an old word and write it down with its meaning.
Make a short poster about Nowruz and how people celebrate it.
Find Kashgar, Balasagun and Baghdad on a modern map.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week that shows a value from the chapter is …

miniProject.title: Mahmud Kashgari: A Museum Exhibition
miniProject.desc: In groups, each member becomes an expert on one part of the book: life, book, map or calendar. Teach your part, then plan four exhibition panels with short labels and one quotation each.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Book That Keeps a Culture Alive
reflectivePrompt.desc: Kashgari’s work can be seen as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture (Chapter 3). Write six to eight sentences about a book, notebook or record that keeps a culture alive in your family or town.

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect: Kashgari names respect for elders among the qualities of the Turks, and he knew Arabic and Persian well while praising Turkish (Chapters 1, 4 and 6).

items.label: D3 Diligence
items.value: Diligence: Kashgari traveled for ten or fifteen years to collect material and improved his work several times (Chapters 3 and 4).

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility: The khan wanted a calendar so that the people after him would not make mistakes about dates (Chapter 8).

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Honesty: The writer separates facts from what is believed or likely (Chapters 2, 5 and 7).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.

content.chapter: Chapter 1: The First Linguistic Study of Turkic
objectives: I can explain what kind of study Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is.
I can say what the work aimed to do.
I can use the passive (was written by) and which for extra information.

content.grammarFocus: Look at “It was written by Mahmud Kashgari”: the passive puts the book first. Then choose which, was and both, and rewrite three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: lin-GUIS-tic, DI-a-lect, KNOWL-edge-a-ble.
content.lessonPlan: Do people in your country speak in different ways? Write one example. Read the chapter and find what a dialect is. Make a definition box for “dialect”.
discussionPoints: Kashgari wanted to show the richness of his language. What is one rich or beautiful thing about your language?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Dictionary of Dialects” and “Turkic to Arabic” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the second paragraph again. Find “It aimed to”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences about a dialect or accent you know.

whatToNotice: The book is the first linguistic study of Turkic.
It was a dictionary from Turkic dialects to Arabic.
readListen: Do people in your country speak in different ways? Write one example.
Read the chapter and find what a dialect is.
Make a definition box for “dialect”.
findAnswerInStory: Find what the study includes.
Find what the work aimed to do.
Find which languages Kashgari knew well.

“The comprehensive content of the work.” What does comprehensive mean?
Write one sentence with knowledgeable.

selfCheck: Can I explain what kind of study it is?
Can I define a dialect?
Can I use the passive?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences about a dialect or accent you know.

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain in three sentences what Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk is and why it was written. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “It aimed to teach the Turkic language to Arabs and prove that it is just as rich as Arabic.” in your home language.

thinkAloud.sentence: A dialect is a regional form of a language with its own special vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “A dialect is” tells me this is a definition. The next sentence starts with “So”, so it uses the definition to explain the book’s title. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “It was written by Mahmud Kashgari in 11th-century Karakhanid Turkish.”
stopAndCheck.question: In which language and century was it written? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can describe where Kashgari was born and died.
I can explain how Kashgari describes himself.
I can use It is generally believed that and one of the + superlative.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “It is generally believed that he was born in Barsgan”: a common view. Then choose best, clearest and throwers, and rewrite three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say: BARS-gan, KASH-gar. Stress: AN-ces-tor.
content.lessonPlan: How would you describe yourself? Write one sentence. Read the chapter and find where Kashgari was born. Make a profile card: born, died, family, skills.
discussionPoints: Kashgari was proud of his family and his language. What are you proud of in your family?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Kashgar” and “Nasr Ilig Khan” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the second sentence again. Find where he was born and where he died. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences describing a person you admire.

whatToNotice: The place of birth is a common view, not complete proof.
Kashgari describes himself with superlatives.
readListen: How would you describe yourself? Write one sentence.
Read the chapter and find where Kashgari was born.
Make a profile card: born, died, family, skills.
findAnswerInStory: Find where Kashgar is today.
Find who his ancestor was.
Find four things he says about himself.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: East Turkestan, belongs to, ancestor, Transoxiana, spear throwers.
“His ancestor was Nasr Ilig Khan.” What is an ancestor?
Write one sentence with belongs to.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will decide if a statement is true or false. Read the second sentence.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find where he was born and where he died.
selfCheck: Can I describe where he was born and died?
Can I explain his family background?
Can I use one of the + superlative?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences describing a person you admire.
content.reflectionPrompt: Kashgari was proud of his family and his language. What are you proud of in your family?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Give a short profile of Mahmud Kashgari. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Kashgari says that he belongs to a noble family, and his ancestor was Nasr Ilig Khan, the famous Karakhanid ruler who conquered Transoxiana and Bukhara.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, who Mahmud Kashgari was and what he said about himself.

thinkAloud.sentence: He also says he is one of the Turks who know the language best, one of the clearest speakers, one of the wisest, and one of the best spear throwers.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “He says” tells me these are Kashgari’s own claims. The pattern “one of the … -est” repeats four times. I can make a list of four qualities. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “Mahmud Kashgari was born in 1008 and died in 1105.”
stopAndCheck.question: Where was he probably born? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can describe how the Dîvân was written and presented.
I can explain why the work can be seen as an encyclopedia.
I can use after + -ing and For this reason.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “after improving it several times”: after + -ing shows the earlier action. Then fill After, In addition and For this reason, and correct three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: en-cy-clo-PE-di-a, PROV-erbs.
content.lessonPlan: What can you find in an encyclopedia? Write two things. Read the chapter and find the three years. Draw a timeline and a mind map.
discussionPoints: Kashgari improved his work several times. Why is it good to check and improve your work?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Baghdad, 1077” and “An Encyclopedia” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the first two sentences again. Find 1072, 1074 and 1077. Order them again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences about a project you finished.

whatToNotice: Kashgari improved the work several times before he completed it.
The work has information about nearly every aspect of life.
readListen: What can you find in an encyclopedia? Write two things.
Read the chapter and find the three years.
Draw a timeline and a mind map.
findAnswerInStory: Find to whom he presented the work.
Find how many words, proverbs and idioms it contains.
Find why it can be seen as an encyclopedia.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: related to.
“Information and practices related to nearly every aspect of life.” What does related to mean?
Write one sentence with proverbs.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put four events in order. Look at the years.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the first two sentences again.
selfCheck: Can I describe the steps in order?
Can I explain why it is like an encyclopedia?
Can I use after + -ing?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences about a project you finished.
content.reflectionPrompt: Kashgari improved his work several times. Why is it good to check and improve your work?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain how the Dîvân was written and why it can be called an encyclopedia. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “For this reason, the work can be seen as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, how Kashgari wrote his book and what it contains.

thinkAloud.sentence: For this reason, the work can be seen as an encyclopedia of Turkic culture.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “For this reason” tells me this is a conclusion. The reason is the long list before it. The book has information about nearly every part of life. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “The work contains about 9,000 Turkic words, proverbs, and idioms.”
stopAndCheck.question: To whom did he present his work in 1077? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can report what Kashgari writes about the Turks.
I can describe his journey and its purpose.
I can use owing to and until for reasons and time.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “Owing to this belief and confidence”: owing to means because of. Then choose states, records and adds, and rewrite three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say: O-ghuz, CHI-gil. Stress: MOD-es-ty, CON-fi-dence.
content.lessonPlan: Why do people travel to learn something? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find what Kashgari writes about the Turks. Make a journey card.
discussionPoints: Kashgari names respect for elders among the qualities of the Turks. How can you show respect to an elder this week?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Journey” and “The Dialects” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the second paragraph again. Find “During this time”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Plan a research trip about language or culture in your region.

whatToNotice: Kashgari reports views and a hadith in his work.
His journey lasted ten or fifteen years.
readListen: Why do people travel to learn something? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find what Kashgari writes about the Turks.
Make a journey card.
findAnswerInStory: Find the good qualities of the Turks.
Find when he left his home.
Find the dialects he learned.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: qualities, long-lasting kingdom, Owing to.
“A long-lasting kingdom.” What does long-lasting mean?
Write one sentence with owing to.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose what he did during his travels. Read the second paragraph.
selfCheck: Can I report his views?
Can I describe his journey?
Can I use owing to and until?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Plan a research trip about language or culture in your region.
content.reflectionPrompt: Kashgari names respect for elders among the qualities of the Turks. How can you show respect to an elder this week?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain Kashgari’s belief about the Turks and how he collected his material. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “During this time, he collected the material that he needed for his work.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, why Kashgari traveled and what he collected.

thinkAloud.strategy: Link a reason and an action
thinkAloud.sentence: Owing to this belief and confidence, he started his journey and began to visit all Turkic countries.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Owing to” means “because of”. “This belief” points back to the hadith. So the hadith is the reason for the journey. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “He then describes many good qualities of the Turks, such as beauty, bright faces, good manners, modesty, bravery, and respect for elders.”
stopAndCheck.question: When did Kashgari leave his home? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Oghuz and the Caliph
objectives: I can explain why the Oghuz get the most attention in the book.
I can name the three great Turkic states of the time.
I can use probably and It is likely that for careful explanations.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “It is likely that Kashgari was aware”: a careful explanation. Then choose why, not and most, and rewrite three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say: SEL-juks, GHAZ-na-vids. Stress: po-LIT-i-cal.
content.lessonPlan: Why do some groups get more attention in history? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find which tribe gets the most attention. Make a cause chart.
discussionPoints: The writer is careful not to say more than he knows. Why is it important to be careful when we explain things?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Oghuz” and “Three Great States” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the second paragraph again. Find “the Seljuks, an Oghuz Turkic tribe”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences explaining why something is popular.

whatToNotice: The writer gives a careful explanation with probably.
The book was finished in Baghdad and given to the caliph.
readListen: Why do some groups get more attention in history? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find which tribe gets the most attention.
Make a cause chart.
findAnswerInStory: Find how many Oghuz tribes Kashgari names.
Find who protected the Abbasids.
Find the three great Turkic states.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: tribes.
“How their tribes were organized.” What is a tribe?
Write one sentence with powerful.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will decide if a statement is true or false. Read the second paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Find “the Seljuks, an Oghuz Turkic tribe”.
selfCheck: Can I explain why the Oghuz get attention?
Can I name the three states?
Can I use It is likely that?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences explaining why something is popular.
content.reflectionPrompt: The writer is careful not to say more than he knows. Why is it important to be careful when we explain things?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain why the Oghuz get so much attention in the book. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “The Oghuz are the Turkic tribe that gets the most attention in the book.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, who the Oghuz were and why Kashgari wrote so much about them.

thinkAloud.sentence: The reason why Kashgari drew so much attention to this tribe is probably that the Seljuks, an Oghuz Turkic tribe, were very strong and protected the Abbasids, the center of the Islamic world.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Probably” tells me this is not a sure fact. The writer gives a good reason, but I should present it as a guess. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “He writes the names of twenty-two of the twenty-four Oghuz tribes.”
stopAndCheck.question: How many Oghuz tribes did he name? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can explain why Kashgari praised Turkish.
I can describe the status of Arabic at that time.
I can use make + person + verb for causes.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “made Kashgari praise his own language”: make + person + base verb. Then choose praise, in and could, and correct three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: DOM-i-nant, com-PETE.
content.lessonPlan: Which languages are used for science today? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find the dominant language. Draw cause and result.
discussionPoints: Kashgari loved his own language and knew other languages well. How can we love our language and respect other languages?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Arabic in Schools” and “His Mother Tongue” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the last sentence again. Find “made Kashgari praise”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences praising your mother tongue.

whatToNotice: Arabic had a very high status at that time.
Kashgari believed Turkish could compete with Arabic.
readListen: Which languages are used for science today? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find the dominant language.
Draw cause and result.
findAnswerInStory: Find where Arabic was the main language.
Find in which language scholars wrote.
Find what Kashgari believed in.
vocabularyInContext: This chapter has no Word Notes.
“Arabic was dominant.” What does dominant mean?
Write one sentence with mother tongue.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose what made Kashgari praise Turkish. Read the last sentence.
selfCheck: Can I explain why he praised Turkish?
Can I describe the status of Arabic?
Can I use make + person + verb?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write four to five sentences praising your mother tongue.
content.reflectionPrompt: Kashgari loved his own language and knew other languages well. How can we love our language and respect other languages?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain why Kashgari praised Turkish. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “The scholars of that time also wrote their books in Arabic.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, why Kashgari wanted to praise his mother tongue.

thinkAloud.sentence: This high status of Arabic made Kashgari praise his own language, Turkish, because he believed in the richness of his mother tongue and that it could compete with Arabic.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “This high status” points back to the first two sentences. “Made … praise” shows a cause and an effect. “Because” adds his personal reason. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “In the schools of the Karakhanid and Transoxiana cultural centers, Arabic was dominant and the main language for teaching.”
stopAndCheck.question: In which language did scholars write their books? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: The Importance of the Map
objectives: I can describe Kashgari’s map and its center.
I can explain how the map reflects Kashgari’s belief.
I can use while for contrast and as far … as for distance.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “…, while China is shown as …”: while compares two facts. Then choose considered, as and to, and rewrite three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say: ba-la-sa-GUN, ja-BAR-qa. Stress: car-TOG-ra-pher.
content.lessonPlan: What is in the center of the maps you know? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find the center of Kashgari’s map. Draw the map with its colors.
discussionPoints: Kashgari’s map also shows the nations that had relations with the Turks. Why is it useful to know about our neighbors?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Balasagun” and “Jabarqa” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the second paragraph again. Find “mountains in red”. Match again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Describe a map of your world, with your town at the center.

whatToNotice: The map reflects Kashgari’s belief about the Turks.
It is the first world map that shows Japan.
readListen: What is in the center of the maps you know? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find the center of Kashgari’s map.
Draw the map with its colors.
findAnswerInStory: Find the city in the heart of the map.
Find how far west the map goes.
Find the old names for Japan and China.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: document.
“From a Turkic geographical perspective.” What is a perspective?
Write one sentence with document.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will match features with colors. Read the second paragraph.
selfCheck: Can I describe the map?
Can I explain how it reflects his belief?
Can I use while?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Describe a map of your world, with your town at the center.
content.reflectionPrompt: Kashgari’s map also shows the nations that had relations with the Turks. Why is it useful to know about our neighbors?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain why Kashgari’s map is important. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “It is likely that he made his map to reflect this belief.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, what Kashgari’s map shows and why it is famous.

thinkAloud.sentence: In the south, they go from the Egyptian border to Ethiopia and India, and they reach China and Japan in the east.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: I follow the directions: south, then east. The sentence before gives the west. I can now say how far the map goes in each direction. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “Because of this map, which is considered the oldest document made from a Turkic geographical perspective, Kashgari is known as the first Turkic cartographer.”
stopAndCheck.question: What is Kashgari known as because of this map? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: The Story of the Calendar
objectives: I can retell the story of the Twelve-Animal calendar.
I can explain the khan’s reason for a calendar.
I can use first conditional sentences and However / Therefore.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “If we make a mistake …, the people after us will also make a mistake”: a real possibility and its result. Then choose However, Therefore and so, and rewrite three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say: ku-rul-TAY. Stress: de-TER-mine, pre-VENT.
content.lessonPlan: How did people remember dates before calendars? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find why the khan wanted a calendar. Put five events in order.
discussionPoints: The khan thought about the people who would live after him. What can we do today for people in the future?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Kurultay” and “The Ili Valley” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter again. Underline the five events. Order them again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Suggest a system that helps your class remember important dates.

whatToNotice: The khan thought about the people after him.
The years got their names from the animals that crossed the river.
readListen: How did people remember dates before calendars? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find why the khan wanted a calendar.
Put five events in order.
findAnswerInStory: Find what the Turks used the calendar to record.
Find what a kurultay was.
Find which animal crossed first.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: chased.
“The people chased them toward the river.” What does chased mean?
Write one sentence with record.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put the legend in order. Start with the second paragraph.
selfCheck: Can I retell the legend?
Can I explain the khan’s reason?
Can I use the first conditional?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Suggest a system that helps your class remember important dates.
content.reflectionPrompt: The khan thought about the people who would live after him. What can we do today for people in the future?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
columns: The river in the Ili Valley
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Tell the story of the twelve-animal calendar in four steps. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “They used this method to record their children’s ages, war dates, and other historical events.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, how the twelve-animal calendar began.

thinkAloud.sentence: Therefore, the calendar starts with the Year of the Rat.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “However, the people around him did not agree on the correct date.”
stopAndCheck.question: Where is the Ili Valley? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

I can match old Turkic names with their English meanings.

Find the old name of each animal.

Find the meaning of Koy.
Find the eleventh year.

“Year of the Leopard.” What is a leopard?
Write one sentence with rooster.

selfCheck: Can I name the twelve years?
Can I match old names and meanings?
Can I use ordinal numbers?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Choose three animals from the list and describe their qualities.
content.reflectionPrompt: Kashgari wrote down old words so that they would not be lost. Which old words in your family are worth keeping?

noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Say the twelve animals in order and two of the old Turkic names. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Year of the Nag means ‘Year of the Crocodile’” in your home language.

metadata.title: Mahmud Kashgari B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study Mahmud Kashgari and his work alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 11 chapters of Mahmud Kashgari.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the life, journey and purpose of Mahmud Kashgari.
Explain the work, the map and the calendar with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 11.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One thing from Dîvânu Lugâti’t-Türk that I would like to see:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 11 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows respect, diligence, responsibility and careful honesty. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Respect: Respect: Kashgari names respect for elders among the qualities of the Turks, and he knew Arabic and Persian well while praising Turkish (Chapters 1, 4 and 6).
Diligence: Diligence: Kashgari traveled for ten or fifteen years to collect material and improved his work several times (Chapters 3 and 4).
Responsibility: Responsibility: The khan wanted a calendar so that the people after him would not make mistakes about dates (Chapter 8).
Honesty: Honesty: The writer separates facts from what is believed or likely (Chapters 2, 5 and 7).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 11, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell someone at home in five sentences who Mahmud Kashgari was and why his work is important, in your home language or in English.
